title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: 55% of primary voters oppose data centers nearby—what it means for bills, water and towns.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Monday, August 3rd, and yesterday's new poll is showing real pushback from voters on these projects landing close to home.
Yeah, 55 percent statewide opposition, jumping to 63 percent among likely Democratic primary voters. That's the big story we're digging into today.
Exactly. This isn't just one poll—it's reflecting fights that have been building for months in places like Saline, Coldwater, and now Genesee County.
Graham, walk me through why this opposition is spiking right now. Is it the power bills, the water, or something else?
It's all of it. Data centers pull massive electricity—hundreds of megawatts for big ones—and that can mean higher rates for everyone if new generation isn't added fast enough.
And the water angle? I've heard residents worry about wells and rivers drying up.
Right. Cooling systems need a lot of water, and in rural townships that already manage tight supplies, folks are asking who pays for upgrades or restrictions.
Farmland is another piece, isn't it? These campuses take up space that could stay agricultural.
Yes, and towns are split—some see tax revenue and jobs, others see noise, traffic, and strain on local grids that weren't built for this scale.
The poll breaks it down by party too. Why do you think Democrats are showing stronger opposition at 63 percent?
Candidates are making it a primary issue. Abdul El-Sayed held a rally Friday in Saline blasting tax breaks and grid strain, saying residents 30 minutes away could see higher rates.
And on the other side, John James told The Detroit News on Saturday he'd leave siting and tax decisions to local officials instead of state rules.
That's a key difference. James is betting voters in data-center counties like those around Coldwater want local control, while El-Sayed is hitting the power and tax deals directly.
Does the poll suggest one approach is resonating more?
It shows broad skepticism overall, with Democrats more opposed. The August 4 primary will test whether James's local-control stance helps or hurts him in those areas.
What about the history here? How long have these clashes been going on?
It's accelerated this year. We've seen pauses in places like Otsego just this weekend, and earlier fights in Saline and Coldwater over the same issues—power, water, and who gets the tax breaks.
So the poll isn't coming out of nowhere—it's the result of months of public meetings and noise complaints.
Right. Dowagiac residents have been dealing with constant high-pitched whine from an existing facility, and that experience is shaping how Cass County looks at new proposals.
What happens next after this poll? Do we see more towns following Otsego's one-year ban?
Possibly. Genesee County already delayed an environmental vote on Saturday, giving residents extra time to review traffic, power, and noise impacts.
And Mason County is pitching itself for the state's official data center. How does that fit with the opposition trend?
It's the flip side—some rural counties want the construction jobs and tax revenue, but they'll still face the same questions on power demand and land use if it moves forward.
Verrus is pushing ahead on a Michigan project while its Salem plans stall. Any word on where that lands?
Not the exact site yet, but local officials are already fielding questions about power and tax deals. Communities are watching closely.
Coldwater residents got their first look at plans on Friday. What stood out in that meeting?
Mainly the same concerns: how much power and water the projects pull and what tax breaks are offered. Similar fights are heating up in nearby townships.
So the poll captures a statewide mood, but the real action stays local.
That's the takeaway. Voters want more say, and candidates are responding with different prescriptions.
Will we see more polling or candidate events on this before the primary?
Likely. The tracker will keep an eye on it—full sources at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
Alright, let's hit the other stories from the weekend quickly.
Saturday brought a big shift at the Dowagiac campus—Hyperscale Data is moving from Bitcoin mining to a 20-megawatt AI contract under a 10-year deal.
That could generate over $1.2 billion, but residents are still litigating the noise from the site.
Exactly. The reallocation shows how fast these facilities can pivot to AI demand.
Genesee County postponed its environmental clearance vote on Saturday too.
Yes, giving Flint-area residents more weeks to weigh in on traffic, power, and industrial noise.
Otsego city council voted Saturday for a full one-year ban on new data centers.
That pause lets residents shape rules on noise and grid strain before anything big hits.
Mason County is bidding to host the state's official data center.
Local leaders see construction jobs and tax revenue, but power demand and land use questions remain for residents.
Coldwater had its joint meeting Friday to brief the public on proposed centers.
Residents there are focused on power, water, and tax breaks—same as everywhere else.
Verrus is advancing its Michigan project despite uncertainty in Salem.
No exact site disclosed yet, but communities are already asking about the demands.
El-Sayed rallied Friday at the Saline site against the AI power deals.
He highlighted tax breaks and potential rate hikes for nearby residents.
And John James's local-control stance from Saturday.
He wants towns like Saline and Coldwater to decide siting and taxes themselves.
Dowagiac noise complaints are still shaping Cass County's approach.
Neighbors describe nonstop high-pitched whine, pushing for stronger rules on future projects.
That's a solid round of quick hits. Now, what's on deck for listeners?
Tonight, Monday August 3, the Delta County Planning Commission has its Data Center Subcommittee update and zoning ordinance discussion.
That sounds like a good one for anyone in the western UP wanting to weigh in on rules.
Exactly—agendas like that are where the local decisions get shaped.
Anything else coming up this week we should flag?
We'll keep tracking the primary fallout and any new meetings. The tracker has the live map.
Perfect. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening—stay informed on Michigan's data center buildout.
